Hollingsworth v. Perry, 570 U.S. 693 (2013), was a landmark United States Supreme Court case that effectively restored same-sex marriage in California. The case began in 2009 when two same-sex couples challenged Proposition 8, a California state constitutional amendment that banned same-sex marriage, under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. In May 2008, the California Supreme Court ruled in In re Marriage Cases that laws restricting marriage to opposite-sex couples violated the state's constitution. As a result, same-sex couples gained the right to marry. However, in November 2008, California voters passed Proposition 8, which reinstated the ban on same-sex marriage by amending the state constitution. Shortly after its passage, several lawsuits were filed to challenge Proposition 8. In Strauss v. Horton (2009), the California Supreme Court upheld Proposition 8, but also ruled that marriages performed before its passage would remain valid. In May 2009, two same-sex couples, Kristin Perry & Sandra Stier and Paul Katami & Jeffrey Zarrillo, filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California challenging Proposition 8 under federal law. The case was led by attorneys David Boies and Theodore Olson, who famously argued opposite sides in Bush v. Gore, the case that decided the 2000 presidential election. In August 2010, Judge Vaughn Walker ruled in Perry v. Schwarzenegger that Proposition 8 violated the U.S. Constitution by denying same-sex couples the fundamental right to marry, thus violating the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. Judge Walker's decision was a landmark ruling that laid the groundwork for further legal battles over marriage equality. The case reached the Supreme Court of the United States in 2013 as Hollingsworth v. Perry. The key issue before the Court was not whether same-sex marriage was constitutional, but whether the proponents of Proposition 8 had the legal standing to defend the law after state officials, including Governor Jerry Brown and Attorney General Kamala Harris, refused to do so. On June 26, 2013, in a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court ruled that the proponents of Proposition 8 did not have legal standing to appeal the lower court's ruling, as they could not demonstrate any direct harm resulting from the decision. The ruling effectively allowed same-sex marriage to resume in California, as the lower court's decision striking down Proposition 8 remained intact. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, joined by Justices Scalia, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Kagan. Justice Anthony Kennedy dissented, arguing that the Court should have ruled on the merits of the case rather than dismissing it for lack of standing. The Supreme Court's decision in Hollingsworth v. Perry paved the way for same-sex marriage to resume in California. On June 28, 2013, same-sex couples began marrying once again in the state. The case was part of a broader legal movement toward marriage equality in the United States, culminating in the landmark 2015 decision in Obergefell v. Hodges, which legalized same-sex marriage nationwide.

Holography is a way of making three-dimensional picture with a laser. It allows the holographer to make a more exact image than with photography. The holograph seems to move and change slightly to look as if it were three-dimensional. Holography uses the wave aspect of light. Holograms are made with light flashed onto a plate or screen, almost like how photos are made. To make a hologram instead of a photograph, some of the light, called a "reference beam," has to go directly to the screen. The light has to be a laser because lasers are more accurate and have a wavelength that does not change the way the wavelengths of light from other sources does, like light from lightbulbs. To stop other light from ruining the hologram, holograms are usually taken in the dark. Because even the tiniest vibration can stop the hologram from forming properly, the tables upon which that the holographer places the equipment may be built with shocks or inflated chambers to stop vibrations from the floor. Holograms can be compared to photos. Holography records the intensity of light, like photography, but also records the difference in the phase of light. Holography records all of information from the light that the object reflects. A hologram records the light that comes from many places, so a person looking at it can see it from many angles. A photo can be made with normal light, like light from the sun or a lightbulb, but holograms can only be made with lasers. A hologram needs a second laser (the reference beam) to go onto the plate or screen where the hologram is being made. When a photo is cut in half, each piece shows half of the photo. When a hologram is cut in half, the entire holograph is shown in each piece. This is because each piece of a photo shows only that part of the photo, but each point on a hologram shows light from all over. Close up, holographs look like a random bunch of bumps. Holography uses a reference wave (which goes onto the plate) and an exposure wave (object wave, which comes from the object). The reference wave can save the phase information as patterns of light and dark on a film. The object wave and reference wave must have the same wavelength in order to save the phase information and they usually come from the same laser. The most famous person in the history of holography is the physician Dennis Gabor, the inventor of the hologram. In 1947, he was trying to improve microscopes, and he figured out how to display three-dimensional objects. 1920: Mieczysław Wolfke proposes principle of wave field reconstruction by diffraction on diffraction patterns 1947: Dennis Gábor develops the principle of holography 1960: Theodor Maiman invents the laser (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) 1963: Emmeth Leith and Juris Upatnieks improve the recording technique 1964: Production of the first hologram by Leith and Upatnieks ("Train and Bird"). 1965: Juri Nikolajewitsch Denisjuk invents white-light-holography 1968: Stephen A. Benton invents the rainbow-transmission holography 1971: Award of the Nobel Prize of physics goes to Dennis Gábor for the invention of holography Holograms need laser beams. A dispersing lens makes the beam bigger and then it goes through a special mirror. Only a piece of this laser beam can go through the mirror. Then this beam becomes the reference wave, and it is recorded on the film. The other piece of the laser beam is reflected off of the mirror. This piece becomes the exposure wave at the object. The object reflects this wave on the film. Making a hologram is very similar to making a photograph, and it needs chemicals. To look at a hologram the film must be lit up with the reference wave. These waves are reflected on the film (hologram) and create a virtual picture of the recorded object, even if that picture can only be seen from a specific angle. Industries use holograms to measure things. In the car industry, cars are measured using holography so engineers can see bulges and vibration characteristics. Phase-shift holography is one kind of holography used to make cars. The first step in making a hologram is to examine the ground level state of the object, then overload the object through heat or mechanical pressure. Covering the original hologram and the modified hologram can produce interference fringes. By measuring the interference fringes, engineers learn how big the deformation or other problem is. Engineers can measure tiny terminal expansions or vibrations in mechanical systems. This needs two reference waves. There are holographic storage machines for analog pictures and digital data. Digital information will be affiliated by a two-dimensional bit-pattern.

Homo erectus (Latin: "upright man") is an extinct species of the genus Homo. Fossil remains were found in Java (1890s) and in China (1921). Nearly all of them were lost during World War II, but there are casts that are considered to be reliable evidence. Early in the 20th century it was believed that the first modern humans lived in Asia. But during the 1950s and 1970s, many fossil finds from East Africa (Kenya) showed that the oldest hominins came from there. H. erectus had a cranial capacity (brain size) greater than the earlier Homo habilis. The earliest H. erectus remains have a cranial capacity of 850 cm³, while the latest Javan specimens measure up to 1100 cm³. This overlaps that of H. sapiens. The frontal bone is less sloped and the dental arcade smaller than in australopithecines. The face is more vertical (less protrusive) than either the australopithecines or H. habilis, with large eyebrow-ridges and less prominent cheekbones. The face is longer than most australopithecines, with a larger brow and smaller cheekbones. Body hair protects the skin from wounds, bites, heat, cold, and UV radiation. Also, it is used as a communication tool and as a camouflage. The first member of the genus Homo to be hairless was Homo erectus, originating about 1.6 million years ago. The most widely accepted explanation is that H. Erectus evolved hairless bodies and increased sweat glands to make it easier for their bodies to cool down. Man's ancestors moved from living in shady forest to open savanna, and they needed to be able to keep cool. This change in environment resulted in a change in diet, from largely vegetarian to hunting. Hunting game on the savanna also increased the need for the body to stay cool. Anthropologist and paleo-biologist Nina Jablonski thinks the ability to lose body heat through sweating helped make possible the dramatic enlargement of the brain. The brain is the most temperature-sensitive human organ. The ability to stay cool allowed the brain to enlarge over time. The loss of fur was also a factor in other adaptations. Some of these changes are thought to be the result of sexual selection. By selecting more hairless mates, humans accelerated changes which were first done by natural selection. Sexual selection may also account for the remaining human hair in the pubic area and armpits, which are sites for pheromones, while hair on the head continued to provide protection from the Sun. Humans had hairless bodies, upright posture, and high brain capacity by 260,000 to 350,000 years ago. These early hominins stood about. Only 17 percent of modern male humans are taller. They were slender, with long arms and legs. The sexual dimorphism between males and females was slightly greater than modern man, with males being about 25% larger than females. The discovery of the skeleton KNM-WT 15000, "Turkana boy" (Homo ergaster), made near Lake Turkana, Kenya by Richard Leakey and Kamoya Kimeu in 1984, is one of the most complete hominid skeletons discovered. It has provided important information about how humans evolved. The most distinctive tool of H. erectus was the Acheulean hand axe, first invented 1.8 million years ago (mya). This hand axe was made by chipping a suitable stone with a hammer stone. Later, the Neanderthals used a soft hammer made of deer antler bone to make better tools. The Acheulean hand axe lasted for over a million years as the main tool. Its main use was for butchering meat. This we know because different uses leave different micro-wear on the hand axe surfaces. Homo erectus remains one of the most successful and long-lived species of the Homo genus. It is generally considered to have given rise to a number of descendant species and subspecies. The oldest known specimen of the ancient human was found in southern Africa. Indonesia (island of Java): Trinil 2 (holotype), Sangiran collection, Sambungmachan collection, Ngandong collection China: Lantian (Gongwangling and Chenjiawo), Yunxian, Zhoukoudian, Nanjing, Hexian India: Narmada (taxonomic status debated!) Kenya: WT 15000 (Nariokotome), ER 3883, ER 3733 Fossil H. erectus skulls found in Java in the 1930s have recently been redated. There are 12 skullcaps (the top part of the skull) and two lower leg bones. The recent research shows that on Java, H. erectus survived to about 100,000 years ago. The research gives a definitive age of between 117,000 and 108,000 years ago. That is much a much longer survival than in any other part of the world, so far as is known. This means, says the report, that H. erectus was still around when our own species was [elsewhere] walking the Earth. Java is an island, and presumably it had not yet been discovered by Neanderthals or our own species. Remains suggest that our own species did not reach Java until about 39,000 years ago.

Hong Wang (; born 1991) is a Chinese mathematician. She is known for her research in Fourier analysis and geometric measure theory. She was awarded the Maryam Mirzakhani New Frontiers Prize in 2022, the Salem Prize in 2025, and the Fields Medal in 2026.

Honoré de Balzac (; born in Tours, France, on 20 May 1799; died in Paris on 18 August 1850) was a French writer. He is often seen as one of the most important writers of novels in the history of literature. He was also one of the first great writers of realism. Realism is a kind of writing that tries to show people and everyday life as they really are. Balzac placed almost all his novels and stories under one title: La Comédie humaine (in English, The Human Comedy). It is a group of about ninety novels and short stories. Together, these books show many parts of French society during the first half of the 19th century. Their characters include nobles and servants, bankers and poor students, priests, soldiers, shopkeepers, artists, criminals, and many other kinds of people. About 2,500 invented characters appear in this world. Many of them return in more than one book. Balzac's own life was almost as full of drama as his novels. He tried to work as a printer, but the business failed. After this, he remained in debt for the rest of his life. This meant that he always owed money. He often wrote during the night, drank very large amounts of coffee, and sometimes worked for fifteen hours a day or more. For almost eighteen years, he loved a Polish countess, Ewelina Hańska. For much of this time, they knew each other mainly through their letters. They finally married in March 1850. Balzac died only five months later, after years of hard work and illness. Balzac became even more famous after his death. Writers such as Gustave Flaubert, Émile Zola, Marcel Proust, Fyodor Dostoyevsky, Henry James, and Oscar Wilde learned from his work. His books can be read for free in French on Wikisource. Balzac was born on 20 May 1799 in Tours, a quiet town on the Loire river. His father, Bernard-François, came from a poor farming family in the Tarn, in southern France. The family's real name was "Balssa". Bernard-François changed it to "Balzac". This new name sounded like the name of an old noble family. He worked hard and gained a better place in society. He became an officer who bought food and other goods for the army. He was also a well-known man in Tours. He was already 52 years old when Honoré was born. Balzac's mother, Anne-Charlotte-Laure Sallambier, came from a very different family. Her parents were Paris shopkeepers who sold cloth and things used for sewing. She was only 21 when Honoré, her first child to live, was born. Her family had chosen her husband for her, and the marriage was not happy. She did not show Honoré much love. Later, Balzac wrote bitterly about her. In one letter, he even said that he had never truly had a mother. Like many babies at that time, Honoré was sent to live with a wet nurse. A wet nurse was a woman who was paid to feed and care for another woman's baby. She lived in the village of Saint-Cyr-sur-Loire, near Tours. Honoré stayed with her until he was four years old. Some writers who have studied his life connect this early separation with an important subject in his books. His novels often show children who do not receive enough love. They also show mothers who love one child more than another. Honoré had two sisters, Laure, born in 1800, and Laurence, born in 1802. He also had a younger brother, Henry, born in 1807. Laure remained close to Honoré throughout his life. She later wrote the first book about him. Henry was their mother's favourite child. Most historians believe that Bernard-François was not Henry's real father. They think his father was Jean de Margonne, a family friend who owned the castle of Saché near Tours. Despite these painful experiences, the Balzac home was not always sad. Pierre Barbéris studied the family's papers. He describes them as a lively and hopeful family who often laughed and joked. They belonged to the growing middle class. The young Honoré did not feel that the world had rejected him. His later dark view of society did not come only from an unhappy childhood. In 1807, when Honoré was eight years old, his family sent him to the well-known school of Vendôme. He was a boarder, which means that he lived at the school. The school was run by former members of the Oratory, a Catholic group that taught children. Its rules were very strict. The pupils stayed there throughout the year, even during the holidays. Their parents rarely visited them. During Balzac's six years at the school, his mother came to see him only twice. School records describe Honoré as a fat, quiet boy with red cheeks. He was often punished. However, the school had a large library, and a kind teacher allowed him to read as much as he wished. Honoré also read in secret, even when he had been locked in a room as a punishment. He read many books about history, philosophy, and religion. An old story says that, between the ages of twelve and fourteen, he wrote a work called the "Treatise on the Will". It was said to be a study of the power of the human mind. However, this work was not really written by the young Balzac. It belongs to Louis Lambert, the main character of Balzac's later novel of the same name. The earliest philosophical notes by Balzac that still exist were written several years later, when he was studying law in Paris. In April 1813, before the school year had ended, his family took him home. He was weak and thin. He also seemed strangely distant, almost like a person walking in his sleep. Perhaps his many hours of secret reading had made him ill. Fresh air and long walks helped him become well again. About twenty years later, Balzac used his memories of Vendôme in his novel Louis Lambert (1832). The novel tells the story of a very gifted boy who writes a secret "Treatise on the Will" while studying at the school. The book mixes Balzac's memories with invented events, but the school in the novel is clearly based on the real school of Vendôme. Balzac wrote this unusual novel far from Paris, at the castle of Saché, in June and July 1832. He had recently been badly hurt when he fell from his carriage. Paris was still troubled by street fighting and by the arrests and punishments that followed it. Pierre Barbéris, who studied this part of Balzac's life closely, describes the novel as a journey back to the deepest sources of Balzac's own life and thought. Balzac first experienced life in Paris without his family. From October 1813 to March 1814, he lived as a boarder at the Ganzer and Beuzelin school. From there, he went to classes at the Lycée Charlemagne. In 1814, Bernard-François received a new job in Paris. At the end of the year, the whole family moved to the capital. Honoré finished his school studies there. In 1816, he began to study law. At the same time, he worked as a clerk for the lawyer Jean-Baptiste Guyonnet de Merville. A clerk was a young office worker. He later worked for Passez, a family friend who was a notary. A notary is a legal officer who prepares official papers such as contracts and wills. In these offices, Balzac saw the hidden side of life in Paris. He learned about family fights over money, secret debts, poor widows, and clever tricks with contracts. He never forgot these experiences. Lawyers, notaries, and money-lenders appear in many of his novels. At the same time, he was already becoming less interested in law. His earliest philosophical notes that still exist come from these years. They discuss the soul and ask whether it continues to live after death. One of these notes was written on the back of a legal paper that the young clerk had prepared himself. Several notes repeat, almost exactly, the free-thinking ideas of the 18th century that his father admired. Balzac completed his law degree in 1819. In the same year, his father was forced to retire. Bernard-François's yearly income fell from about 7,800 francs to less than 1,700. The family left Paris and moved to the cheaper village of Villeparisis. His parents wanted Honoré to become a notary, but he refused. He wanted to become a writer. After many family arguments, his parents agreed to let him try. For about two years, they would give him a small amount of help while he tried to begin a literary career. A later story says that Balzac received 1,500 francs each year. Pierre Barbéris showed that this was probably not true. The family had recently lost most of its income and could not have paid so much. Honoré received small packages, clean clothes, and useful help from home. His family also watched his spending very closely. The plan was kept secret. Friends and relations were told that Honoré was living with his family in Albi, in southern France, where his father had been born. In reality, he moved into a cold, small room under the roof at 9 rue Lesdiguières, near the Bastille. There he began to write. His first large project was Cromwell, a tragedy in verse. This was a serious play written in poetry. Balzac worked on it for several months. In May 1820, he read it to his family and some of their friends. The reading was a complete failure. The family asked Andrieux, a professor at the Collège de France, to give his opinion. Andrieux had once taught Laure's new husband, the engineer Surville, at the École polytechnique. In September, the play was also read to Lafon, an actor from the Théâtre-Français. Andrieux said that the young man could choose any career he wished, except literature. Balzac refused to accept this judgment. In fact, he was already becoming more interested in novels than in drama. Around August 1820, he had started a novel called Falthurne. Soon afterwards, he began Sténie, an unfinished story written as a group of letters and set in Tours. In it, he wrote about the "children of the century and of liberty". This was many years before Musset used the famous title Confession of a Child of the Century in 1836. After his serious play failed, Balzac turned to popular fiction. From about 1820 to 1822, he worked with another young writer, Auguste Lepoitevin de l'Égreville. From 1823 to 1825, he worked with Horace Raisson. Both men produced fast and cheap novels for the popular market. Between 1822 and 1825, Balzac published many novels under invented names. The names he used most often were "Lord R'Hoone", made by changing the order of the letters in "Honoré", and "Horace de Saint-Aubin". He did not choose these false names entirely by himself. His mother did not want the family name to appear on the books. Even in 1829, Balzac still hesitated before putting his real name on his first serious novel. These early books followed popular forms. Some were dark stories about castles. Others were comic adventures or copies of the style of the Scottish novelist Walter Scott. The business soon began to bring in money. Early in 1822, Balzac sold three novels to the publisher Hubert. He received first 800 francs, then 1,000, and finally 2,000 francs. He happily wrote to his sister that "Lord R'Hoone" would soon become a fashionable writer, famous for producing many books and loved by women readers. Balzac himself did not think highly of these novels. In a letter to his sister, he called one of them "literary rubbish". Later, he refused to publish them under his own name. However, they were useful training. By writing them, Balzac learned how to build a plot, keep a story moving, and work very quickly. Some ideas from these forgotten books later returned in much better form in his mature novels. Pierre Barbéris studied all these early novels closely. He believed that they were the first testing ground for Balzac's later world. In Le Vicaire des Ardennes (1822), a girl called Annette gives her savings to her cousin Charles, who later betrays her. This story already contains the main idea of Eugénie Grandet. In Wann-Chlore, which Balzac began in 1822, the bitter Madame d'Arneuse is clearly based on Balzac's own mother. The pirate Argow, who is loved and forgiven by an innocent young woman, also points forward to the great criminals and outsiders of La Comédie humaine. During these years, Balzac also met Laure de Berny, the first great love of his life. She was married and twenty-two years older than he was. Their love affair began in 1822. She became his adviser, taught him about high society, lent him money, and remained his most loyal friend. Balzac called her "la Dilecta", meaning "the chosen woman". She stayed close to him until she died in 1836. Balzac later said that without her, he would have died. In 1825, Balzac left literature for business. He became a publisher. His plan was modern and sensible. He wanted to publish the complete works of classic writers such as Molière and La Fontaine in single, cheap books. However, the books did not sell. In 1826, he began a larger business. With a partner, André Barbier, he bought a printing shop in the rue des Marais-Saint-Germain in Paris, now called the rue Visconti. Balzac received the official licence, moved into rooms above the shop, and managed seven printing presses and thirty-six workers. In 1827, he added another business: a type foundry, a workshop that made metal letters for printing. However, he never stopped writing completely. One of the first books recorded as being printed on his presses, in June 1826, was a work of his own. It was a short first version of the Physiologie du mariage. Balzac printed it only to test his new equipment. It was never sold to the public, and perhaps only one copy still exists. The public version, published in 1829, was twice as long. His printing shop also produced the Annales romantiques, a small yearly book connected with the new Romantic movement. Balzac was not a good businessman. He signed too many promises to pay money, borrowed from many people, and spent money on expensive furniture while his workers waited for their wages. The French economy was also going through a crisis, and many companies failed during these years. In 1828, Balzac's businesses collapsed. His mother and Madame de Berny paid part of his debts. Even after the final accounts were completed, he still owed about 60,000 francs. This was a very large amount, and much of it was owed to members of his own family. Balzac never completely escaped from this debt. During the rest of his life, new spending and new loans continued to increase it. However, the failure gave him two kinds of useful knowledge. First, he now understood the world of money from direct experience. He knew about bills, loans, interest, and bankruptcy. Bankruptcy is the legal condition of a person or business that cannot pay its debts. This knowledge appears throughout his novels. Second, the printing shop later returned in his fiction. His great novel Illusions perdues begins inside a small printing house in the provinces. Balzac describes it with the knowledge of someone who had worked in the trade himself. The story also had an unexpected ending. Madame de Berny's young son Alexandre took control of the type foundry. It later became the successful company Deberny et Peignot, which continued in business until 1972. Balzac was ruined at the age of twenty-nine. He returned to the only work he believed he could do: writing. This time, he prepared his books more carefully. In 1828, he travelled to Brittany in western France. He wanted to study the places and memories connected with the Chouan wars. These were royalist uprisings against the French Revolution. He stayed in Fougères with the baron de Pommereul, a retired general whose father had been a friend of Balzac's father. Balzac explained that a play could be created in Paris with cottages made of painted cardboard. A novel, however, needed real places and real landscapes that the writer had seen. Many Romantic writers of the time laughed at the idea of travelling simply to observe a place. Balzac travelled and studied it carefully. This journey was an early example of the documentary method that he later used throughout his career. This method was based on real places and facts. The result was Le Dernier Chouan, later called Les Chouans. It was a historical novel written in the style of Walter Scott. In an early version of the foreword, Balzac created one last false identity. He called himself "Victor Morillon", a poor dreamer from the country around Vendôme who had taught himself everything. The invented life of Morillon already points forward to the character Louis Lambert. Balzac then removed this false name. He signed a contract with the publisher Urbain Canel in January 1829. The contract paid him 1,000 francs. This was only half the amount that one of his earlier novels under a false name had earned. The book appeared in four small volumes in the middle of March 1829. For the first time, Balzac signed a novel with his real name. The book sold slowly, but serious readers noticed it. In June of the same year, his father Bernard-François died. At the end of 1829, Balzac published the Physiologie du mariage, or "Physiology of Marriage", without his name. It is a clever and daring study of marriage, love, and unfaithfulness. It became a subject of conversation in the fashionable salons of Paris. In 1830, he published the Scènes de la vie privée, or "Scenes of Private Life". This was a group of six short works about women, marriage, and family life. Readers, especially women, discovered a writer who seemed to understand the hidden parts of their lives. Balzac had found his public. In August 1831, Balzac published La Peau de chagrin, known in English as The Wild Ass's Skin or The Magic Skin. It tells the story of a young man who receives a magic piece of skin. The skin grants every wish he makes. However, it becomes smaller after each wish, and his remaining life becomes shorter with it. The novel was a great success. It made Balzac famous. It also presented one of his most important ideas: desire uses up life itself. The first readers also saw the novel as a picture of their own time. In January 1831, Balzac was writing "Letters on Paris" for the newspaper Le Voleur. In one of these letters, he discussed the books published during the previous year. He chose four works: his own Physiologie du mariage, Stendhal's Le Rouge et le Noir, Jules Janin's La Confession, and Charles Nodier's Histoire du roi de Bohême. He wrote that these books carried the smell of a dying society. He gave them a new name: the "school of disenchantment". Disenchantment means losing hope and faith in old beliefs. In July 1830, a revolution had removed King Charles X. However, the new government soon disappointed many of the young people who had helped to create it. For Pierre Barbéris, La Peau de chagrin, written soon after this disappointment, became the clearest and most complete work of the school that Balzac had named. It is also the first novel in which a young man called Rastignac appears. Around this time, Honoré Balzac began to call himself Honoré "de" Balzac, as though he came from the aristocracy. He behaved like a dandy, a man who pays great attention to elegant clothes and manners. He bought expensive clothes from a fashionable tailor. He also bought a carriage, walking sticks covered with jewels, and meals in the best restaurants. He collected old furniture and works of art. Almost everything was bought on credit. His debts grew as quickly as his fame. Balzac even created a theory of dandyism. In the autumn of 1830, he published the Traité de la vie élégante, or "Treatise on Elegant Life", in the fashion paper La Mode. The work reads clothes and manners as a language of signs. It is partly serious and partly comic. Barbéris finds a quiet sadness below the jokes. The dandy was also a child of a century that gave strong young men no useful place for their energy. Behind this show of wealth, Balzac worked at an extraordinary speed. Le Colonel Chabert (1832) tells of a soldier of Napoleon who returns after being believed dead. He finds that the new society has no place for him. Le Curé de Tours (1832) describes a small but bitter struggle between priests in a quiet town. Balzac then wrote Louis Lambert (1832) and Eugénie Grandet (1833). The second novel tells the story of a rich miser and his gentle daughter in Saumur. A miser is a person who loves money and hates spending it. Balzac also wrote the Contes drolatiques, or "Droll Stories", between 1832 and 1837. These are comic and openly sexual stories written in a style that copies old French and the works of Rabelais. In December 1834, Balzac described his life in a letter to his friend Zulma Carraud. He said that he slept for five hours and worked for eighteen hours each day. The great flow of work carrying him forward had never moved so quickly. At the beginning of 1835, he was so tired that he sometimes slept for seventeen hours. However, readers greatly admired the novel he was then writing. It was Le Père Goriot. During the summer of 1830, Balzac was far from Paris. He was staying with Madame de Berny at La Grenadière, a small country house above the Loire near Tours. From there, he followed the July Revolution from a distance. During three days of fighting in the streets of Paris, King Charles X was driven from power and Louis Philippe I became king. On 25 July, Charles X signed the orders that caused the crisis. On the same day, Balzac was walking through the countryside to visit his friends, the Margonne family, at Saché. During the walk, he stopped at a poor cottage and asked an old woman for some milk. The woman was caring for abandoned children as though they were her own. Her simple kindness moved him deeply. Balzac described the meeting in a short work called "Scène de village", or "Village Scene". It was not published during his life, but he later used it in Le Médecin de campagne. Pierre Barbéris sees this walk in July as one of the first beginnings of the Scenes of Country Life. While newspapers and politicians fought over power, Balzac had met another France: a world of poor and quiet people who were almost never noticed by the great movement of history. After returning to Paris, Balzac wrote many political articles. At this time, his ideas were still generally liberal. Between September 1830 and March 1831, he published a series called "Lettres sur Paris", or "Letters on Paris", in Le Voleur. In these letters, he followed the new government from week to week and gave his opinions about it. His tone became colder and more critical with each letter. He complained that France was being ruled by tired old men. He also made a prediction. The new government would soon raise the same questions that Charles X had raised. Charles X had raised them in the name of royal power. The new government would raise them in the name of liberty. Balzac also hoped to win a seat in parliament. Before the elections of 1831, he published a short political book called the Enquête sur la politique de deux ministères. He sent forty copies to his old friend, the baron de Pommereul, because he hoped to become a candidate in the area of Fougères. He also considered standing at Cambrai. In Tours, royalists asked him to become their candidate. He refused, even though he was neither a republican nor a supporter of the government. None of these plans led to an election campaign. The legitimists wanted to restore the old royal family. Balzac first moved toward them at the very end of 1831. In the spring of 1832, the change became public. He began to write for their new newspaper, Le Rénovateur. His first article for the paper, published in March 1832, protested against a plan to destroy the monument to the murdered duke of Berry. The scholar Bernard Guyon studied Balzac's political change year by year. He argued that it was not a sudden emotional decision. It was a careful and practical choice. Balzac believed that a writer who wanted a political career needed the support of an organized party. The royalist party was weak and needed new talent. Balzac thought that it would give him an important place more quickly than the liberal side, which was already full of ambitious men. His new friend, the marquise de Castries, was the niece of the duke of Fitz-James, an important legitimist leader. Guyon believed that she supported and strengthened Balzac's decision, but that she did not create it. Barbéris points to another fact that makes the situation more complex. During the same months, Balzac continued to sell strong articles attacking the government to La Caricature, a newspaper of the left. In 1832, therefore, two political sides of Balzac existed together: a royalist side and a rebellious side close to the left. Barbéris argues that Balzac's royalism was mainly a position from which he could fight the government. It gave him a way to attack the new power of money. It was very different from the sad royalism of old nobles who only wished to return to the past. Balzac's royalism remained practical rather than emotional. In May and June 1832, Le Rénovateur published his Essai sur la situation du parti royaliste, or "Essay on the Situation of the Royalist Party". He told the royalists that they had to face the problems of the 19th century as modern problems. In September 1832, he wrote another article for the same paper, called "Du Gouvernement moderne", or "On Modern Government". In this article, he went further. The idea that the old royal family had a natural right to rule might seem absurd, he wrote. However, even if legitimacy did not exist, it would have to be invented. He saw it as a useful way to give government strength and stability. Le Rénovateur thought the article was too daring and did not publish it. It first appeared only in 1933. Barbéris reads it as an argument for a strong, well-managed, and open society, written under royalist language. In such a society, Balzac wrote, social classes should not be closed walls. They should be open fields of competition that anyone could enter. In this way, no human energy would be wasted. Balzac never received an opportunity to stand in an election. In June 1832, while staying at Saché, he discussed with his friend Margonne the possibility of becoming a candidate at Chinon. Like his earlier political plans, this idea came to nothing. He never stood for parliament during the July Monarchy. In private, Balzac was less sure of himself than he appeared in public. In June 1832, he wrote openly to his friend Zulma Carraud. He said that he threw himself into political storms and the dry winds of literary fame because he had not been given the simple happiness of being loved. After this period, Balzac placed more of his political ideas inside his novels. The first important example was Le Médecin de campagne (1833). He had partly planned it as a book that could help him win voters. Barbéris gives the book a more personal meaning. The year 1832 had brought Balzac accidents, political failure, and loneliness. Le Médecin de campagne was his way of recovering. Its hero, Doctor Bénassis, improves the life of a poor mountain village. He is the first major character in Balzac's work who builds something useful instead of only suffering or fighting against society. Balzac offered himself as a candidate again in 1848, but once more he was not elected. Balzac wrote Le Père Goriot, or "Old Goriot", very quickly between September 1834 and January 1835. It first appeared in a magazine. The novel takes place in a poor and dirty boarding house in Paris called the Pension Vauquer. Three people who live there are especially important. Old Goriot is a retired maker of pasta who has given everything he owns to his two selfish daughters. Eugène de Rastignac is a poor young student from southern France who wants to rise in society. Vautrin is a strange and powerful man who is really an escaped convict. At the end of the novel, Goriot dies almost alone. Rastignac stands on the heights of the Père Lachaise cemetery and looks down at Paris. He gives his famous challenge to the city: from now on, the struggle is between Paris and himself. However, this challenge is not the last sentence of the novel. Balzac added another sentence and made it stronger in later editions. Rastignac has just declared war on society. His first act in this war is to go to dinner with Madame de Nucingen, one of Goriot's own daughters. Pierre Barbéris studied the manuscript and Balzac's corrections. He believed that this ending contains the main meaning of the novel. Rastignac's revolt does not free him from the corrupt world. It takes him directly to the tables where its rich members eat. While writing the novel, Balzac developed one of the most important ideas of his career: characters would return. The same invented people would appear in different novels at different times in their lives. For example, Rastignac had already appeared as an older man in La Peau de chagrin. In Le Père Goriot, readers saw him as a young student. Vautrin would return in later novels under different names. Balzac was very excited by this idea. According to a story told by his family, he ran to his sister's home and announced that he was becoming a genius. The manuscript shows the exact moment when he made this decision. At first, Balzac called the student "Massiac". While writing, he crossed out this name and replaced it with "Rastignac", the name of a character who already appeared in another work. Rastignac's family was partly based on Balzac's own family. A letter that Rastignac receives from his sister Laure closely follows a real letter written to Balzac by his sister Laurence in October 1819. From this time, Balzac's separate novels slowly became parts of one enormous connected work. The return of characters became one of the main ideas behind La Comédie humaine. Women were central to Balzac's life and to his letters. After Madame de Berny, he became close to the duchess of Abrantès. She was the widow of one of Napoleon's generals and told Balzac many stories about the Empire. In 1832, he was deeply hurt by the marquise de Castries. She was an important noblewoman who had helped move him toward the royalist party. She encouraged his love, allowed him to follow her to Aix-les-Bains and Geneva, and then refused him. Balzac later took revenge through fiction. In La Duchesse de Langeais (1834), a proud noblewoman plays with the love of an honest soldier and suffers terribly as a result. On 28 February 1832, Balzac received a letter from Odessa. It was signed only "L'Étrangère", meaning "the Stranger" or "the Foreign Woman". The writer was Ewelina Hańska, a Polish countess. She lived with her much older husband on a very large estate at Wierzchownia in Ukraine, which was then part of the Russian Empire. She admired Balzac's books. However, she feared that his recent writing was less morally pure than his early Scènes de la vie privée. Balzac answered her, and a very long exchange of letters began. He continued writing to her for the rest of his life. Of these letters, 414 still exist. Together, they are about one quarter as long as the whole of La Comédie humaine. They are among the best sources for understanding his life and the way he worked. Balzac and Ewelina first met in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, in September 1833. They met again in Geneva during the winter. They became lovers on 26 January 1834. They met once more in Vienna in 1835. After that, they did not see one another for eight years and could communicate only by letter. Ewelina was married, rich, careful, and far away. Balzac dreamed that her elderly husband would die and that she would finally be free to marry him. Balzac also had other, less public relationships. He almost certainly had a daughter with Maria Du Fresnay, a young married woman who admired him. The child, Marie, was born in 1834. Balzac continued to know the family and mentioned Marie in his will. Stories also connected him with several other women. However, work filled more of his nights than love did. Fame did not make Balzac's life peaceful. In 1836, he lost a large amount of money on the Chronique de Paris, a newspaper that he had bought and directed. In the following year, he only just avoided being sent to prison for debt. Madame de Berny died in July 1836. Balzac had just completed Le Lys dans la vallée, or "The Lily of the Valley". Its pure and unhappy heroine, Madame de Mortsauf, was partly based on Madame de Berny. In the same year, Balzac tried a new form of publication. His short novel La Vieille Fille, or "The Old Maid", appeared in separate parts, day after day, in a French daily newspaper. It is often called the first French novel to be published in this way. This new form, called the serial novel, changed literature. Balzac helped to develop it, and it soon controlled much of his working life. Many of his later novels had to be written under the pressure of daily publication dates. Balzac never stopped hoping to make a quick fortune. In 1838, he travelled to Sardinia because he believed that ancient Roman silver mines could be opened again. The plan was not foolish. The mines later made money, but another person had already obtained the right to work them. Balzac returned home with even less money. He then spent large sums on Les Jardies, a small country house at Sèvres near Paris. Among his many plans, he imagined growing pineapples there and selling them in Paris. The house itself cost him about 50,000 francs in 1839. To hide from the people to whom he owed money, Balzac sometimes used false names. From October 1840, he rented rooms in the village of Passy near Paris. The house had a hidden back door that allowed him to escape visitors. He lived there for seven years. It is the only one of his homes in Paris that still exists. It is now the Maison de Balzac museum at 47 rue Raynouard. In 1839, Balzac became president of the Société des gens de lettres, a new association of French writers. He worked to protect the rights of authors. He wanted strong laws to protect literary property. Literary property is the idea that a written work belongs to its author. Balzac also fought newspapers that copied and printed books without paying the writers. His public letters about these questions helped prepare the later development of copyright law in France. He also tried to save a notary called Peytel, who had been sentenced to death for murder. Balzac believed that he was innocent and wrote publicly in his defence. His efforts failed. Balzac also wanted to succeed in the theatre, but most of his plays failed. His play Vautrin opened in Paris on 14 March 1840. The famous actor Frédérick Lemaître played the main part. In the fourth act, Lemaître appeared in a wig that made him look like King Louis Philippe. The king's son left the theatre in anger. The government banned the play the next day. Several of Balzac's other plays failed or were refused by theatres. Critics usually consider Le Faiseur, also called Mercadet, to be his best comedy. It tells the story of a brilliant debtor who uses clever tricks against his creditors, the people to whom he owes money. The play became successful only in 1851, after Balzac had died. In 1840, Balzac made another attempt to succeed in journalism. He wrote almost all of three issues of a magazine called the Revue parisienne. The magazine lost money. However, critics still see some of its articles as among the best literary criticism of the 19th century. The most famous example is Balzac's long and generous study of Stendhal's La Chartreuse de Parme. Balzac praised the novel at a time when very few people understood how great Stendhal was. By 1840, Balzac had written many novels and stories. He understood that they formed one great picture of society. He searched for a title for the whole work and chose La Comédie humaine, or "The Human Comedy". The title answers the Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri. Dante had described a journey through hell, purgatory, and heaven. Balzac would describe a journey through modern society. In October 1841, Balzac signed a contract with a group of publishers led by Furne. They planned to publish a complete and organized edition of his works under the new title. The first volumes appeared in 1842. They opened with the famous "Avant-propos", or foreword, in which Balzac explained the complete plan of his work. By 1848, the Furne edition had grown to seventeen volumes. Balzac continued to correct his personal copy until the end of his life. Scholars call this copy the "Furne corrigé". Modern editions of La Comédie humaine are largely based on it. In November 1841, Ewelina Hańska's husband, Wacław Hański, died in Ukraine. Balzac learned about the death early in 1842. Ewelina was now free to marry. Balzac gave himself one final great aim: he wanted her to become his wife. Ewelina did not agree to marry Balzac immediately. She had a daughter whose future marriage had to be arranged, and she wanted to protect her wealth. She also had doubts about Balzac, who spent money more quickly than he earned it. In 1843, Balzac travelled to Saint Petersburg to meet her after eight years apart. In 1845 and 1846, they travelled together through Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, and Italy. In 1846, Ewelina became pregnant. Balzac was very happy and had already chosen the name Victor-Honoré for the child. However, the baby was born dead at the end of the year. People close to Balzac believed that he never fully recovered from this loss. Despite these difficulties, Balzac continued to write. The complete Illusions perdues, or "Lost Illusions", appeared in three parts between 1837 and 1843. The novel tells the story of Lucien de Rubempré, a handsome but weak young poet from the provinces. Paris and the dishonest world of newspapers destroy him. The story continues in Splendeurs et misères des courtisanes, or "The Splendors and Miseries of Courtesans", which Balzac finished in 1847. Lucien enters a darker Paris ruled by police officers, bankers, and hidden powers. Vautrin controls much of this world from the shadows. In 1846 and 1847, Balzac published the two novels known as the Parents pauvres, or "Poor Relations". La Cousine Bette tells the story of a poor and jealous cousin who secretly destroys her rich relatives. Le Cousin Pons tells the story of a gentle old music lover. His valuable collection of art awakens the greed of everyone around him. La Cousine Bette, which was published in parts in a daily newspaper, was the last great popular success of Balzac's life. His health was now becoming very poor. Many years of working at night, drinking coffee, and worrying about money had damaged his heart. In September 1847, he made his first long journey to Wierzchownia, Ewelina's home in Ukraine. He returned to Paris in February 1848 and saw the revolution that ended the July Monarchy. He even watched the crowd enter the Tuileries palace. In the autumn of 1848, he returned to Ukraine. He stayed there for a year and a half and was seriously ill. Doctors found that he had severe heart disease. He also suffered from bronchitis and problems with his eyes. He could hardly write any longer. Balzac and Ewelina finally married on 14 March 1850. The wedding took place in the church of Saint Barbara in Berdychiv, a town in Ukraine. Balzac was already very ill. At the end of April, the couple began the long and painful journey back across Europe. They reached Paris late during the night of 20 to 21 May 1850. Their arrival became like a scene from one of Balzac's darkest stories. He had prepared a splendid house for Ewelina in the rue Fortunée in Paris. It was filled with works of art, flowers, and lights. However, when they arrived during the night, nobody opened the door. The servant who had been left in charge had become mentally ill. He had damaged parts of the house and locked himself inside. A locksmith had to open the door so that the exhausted couple could enter their own home. Balzac lived for less than three more months.

Honoré Blanc (1736–1807) was a French gunsmith and inventor. He was one of the first to use the concept of interchangeable parts. Blanc was born in Avignon, France in 1736. At age 12 he became an apprentice to a gunsmith. He was an armorer at the Charleville armory in Charleville-Mézières, Ardennes, France. In 1763 he became the controller of gunlocks at the Saint-Étienne arms factory. Just before the French Revolution, he came up with the idea of interchangeable parts for gun locks. By the 1760s, Blanc was making specialized machinery and tools to make gunlocks. His design for the Musket Model 1777 was accepted and he was made chief controller for three arms factories. In 1785, in an experiment, Blanc mixed parts from 25 gunlocks and assembled several models with ease. His demonstration showed the benefit of interchangeable parts and how it worked. He repeated the experiment for military policy makers in 1790. The French Academy of Sciences supported his idea in 1791. But the Legislative assembly would not fund his work. Blanc shifted his attention to setting up a private company to produce gunlocks using interchangeable parts in 1791. Even after receiving permission and funds from the French government, he was very slow in getting started. He did not produce any gunlocks until 1796. His factory was still making gunlocks in 1807 when Blanc died. While European gunsmiths were not impressed by the idea, he did interest the American Ambassador to France, Thomas Jefferson. Jefferson quickly saw that mass production of weapons parts would free America from dependence on European sources for parts. He could not get Blanc to move to the United States but he did convince President George Washington it was a good idea. In 1798, Eli Whitney got the first contract for 10,000 muskets to be delivered within two years. Whitney used a large force of unskilled workers and machinery to produce standardized identical parts at a low cost. This was the first time in the US Blanc's ideas of mass production were put to use. Congress had already decided to pattern the new musket after the 1763 French Charleville musket. This was one that Blanc had worked on early in his career. What resulted was the Springfield Model 1795 Musket, the first military musket made in the United States.

Quintus Horatius Flaccus (December 8, 65 BC - November 27, 8 BC), known to English speakers as Horace, was a famous poet in the Roman Empire. Horace was born in the small Italian town of Venusia. His father used to be a slave, but was known as a freedman because his master had freed him. They moved to Rome a short time later. Horace's father had a job taking items from the seller to the buyer. He received money from these sales. His father became richer and was able to send Horace to the best schools in Rome. He was also able to send him to Athens (Greece) to study the Greek language and philosophy. Horace's native language was Latin. Horace was incredibly proud of his father, and said he felt no shame in being the son of a freedman. In his early adult life, Julius Caesar, the Roman dictator, was killed. War was declared against the people who killed him. Horace joined the army. When the war was over, Horace returned to Italy to find that other people were living in his apartment. His father was also gone. Horace became very poor. Eventually, he found a job in the treasury. This involved sorting the country's money. His friends, Lucius Varius Rufus and Virgil, who were also writers, introduced him to Maecenas. Maecenas was a close friend of Augustus, the emperor of Rome. Horace lived in Tivoli, an area of Rome. When he died, he gave the land he owned to Augustus, to increase the land the state owned. Today, other writers visit the land to remember him. Horace wrote many famous quotes in his poems. These lines are still spoken today, by speakers of every language, in the original Latin. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori - It is sweet and fitting to die for one's country. Carpe diem - Pluck the day (Seize the day is the common translation, though it is incorrect in terms of translation and usage). Some of Horace's poems are difficult to translate because of their syntax, grammar and structure, which is sometimes very different to modern languages. Horace is viewed by many people, including experts, to be one of the best Latin poets.

Horacio Ferrer (June 2, 1933 - December 21, 2014) is a Uruguayan poet, broadcaster, reciter and tango lyricist. He is known for the lyrics he wrote for Astor Piazzolla’s tangos such as Balada para un loco and Chiquilín de Bachín.

Horacio Fidel Cardo (May 20, 1944 – October 22, 2018) was an Argentine painter and illustrator. He was born in Buenos Aires. He not only created paintings and three-dimensional works, but also focused on humour, drawing, and book illustration. From 1983 to 2007, he worked regularly as a freelancer in The New York Times. From 1994 onward, he worked as freelancer with the International Herald Tribune (The Global Edition of the New York Times). Cardo died in Buenos Aires on October 22, 2018 of stomach cancer at the age of 74.

Horace Basil Barlow FRS (8 December 1921 – 5 July 2020) was an Australian visual neuroscientist. In 1953, Barlow discovered that the frog brain has neurons. Barlow also worked in the field of factorial codes. His work was important in the field of statistics of natural scenes. He was elected a member of the Academia Europaea in 1992. Barlow died on 5 July 2020, aged 98.

Horatio Gates Spafford (October 20, 1828, Troy, New York – October 16, 1888, Jerusalem) was a prominent American lawyer and Presbyterian church elder. He is best known for penning the Christian hymn "It Is Well With My Soul". Horatio was a lawyer in Chicago. He lost all of his possessions in the great Chicago fire. After that, he lost his only son to a disease at the age of four. He then planned a family holiday and was held up for business reasons. His family went ahead any way, on the ship all four of his daughters died and his wife survived.

Horst Paulmann Kemna (22 March 1935 – 11 March 2025) was a German-Chilean billionaire entrepreneur. He is founder and chairman of Cencosud, the largest retail chain in Chile and the third largest in Latin America. According to Forbes, his fortune is estimated at US$4.8 billion, and the second richest man in Chile.

Horst Ludwig Störmer (born April 6, 1949) is a German physicist. He is a emeritus professor at Columbia University. He was awarded the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physics jointly with Daniel Tsui and Robert B. Laughlin "for their discovery of a new form of quantum fluid with fractionally charged excitations", also known as the fractional quantum Hall effect.

Horst Nemec (25 January 1939 – 23 June 1984) was an Austrian football forward. He played for Austria Wien and Vienna and the Austrian national football team. Horst Nemec began his football career in August 1950 at Rudolfsheimer AC and came to Austria via SC Helfort Wien. He made his debut in Austria in the 1957–58 season. The striker was able to dominate the championship in Austria and won the championship three times from 1961 to 1963. In this time he was three times top scorer of the league. 1966 he went to Vienna. In 1969 he ended his career. In his career he played 220 league matches and scored 146 goals. He debuted in the national team on 23 September 1959 in a 5:2 win over Norway. In this match he scored his first two international goals. His last match was on 5 September 1965 versus Hungary. He played 29 matches for Austria and scored 16 goals. Scores and results list Austria's goal tally first, score column indicates score after each Nemec goal. In the early 1970s he coached Rosenhügel. After his career, Nemec ran an espresso on Gumpendorfer Strasse in Vienna. He died in 1984 at the age of 45.

Horst Ludwig Georg Erich Wessel (9 October 1907-23 February 1930) was a member of the SA, of the National Socialist German Worker’s Party from 1926-1930. In 1930, he was killed by a communist. As he had written the Horst Wessel-Lied, the party made him into a martyr and hero. Horst Wessel was born in 9 October 1907 in the city of Bielefeld in the Kingdom of Prussia in the German Empire (now; North Rhine-Westphalia). He joined the National Socialist (Nazi Party) in 1926 at the age of 19 he later became Sturmfuhrer of the SA the same year. In February 1930 he was killed by the Communist Party of Germany in Berlin (aged; 22).
Horst Schumann (1 May 1906 in Halle an der Saale – 5 May 1983 in Frankfurt am Main) was an Nazi doctor who did human experiments on prisoners at a concentration camp.

Horst Mahler (; 23 January 1936 – 27 July 2025) was a German lawyer and political activist. He was a far-left militant and a founding member of the Red Army Faction. He later became a supporter of neo-Nazism. Between 2000 and 2003, he was a member of the far-right National Democratic Party of Germany. Starting in 2003, he was convicted of Holocaust denial and served a twelve-year prison sentence. In April 2017, Mahler was ordered back to prison for another three and a half years. On 18 April 2017, he tried to escape from Germany to avoid prison. He was deported back to Germany, where he was arrested and put back in jail. Mahler was released from prison in October 2020. Mahler died on 27 July 2025 in Berlin, Germany at the age of 89.

Albert Horton Foote, Jr. (March 14, 1916 – March 4, 2009) was an American playwright and screenwriter. He was best known for his screenplays for the 1962 movei To Kill a Mockingbird and the 1983 movie Tender Mercies. He was born in Wharton, Texas. He won two Academy Awards (1962, 1983), a Pulitzer Prize (1995) and an Emmy Award (1997). Foote died of natural causes in Hartford, Connecticut at the age of 92.
Hossein Abarghouei (; born September 17, 1997) is an Iranian football midfielder who currently plays for Iranian football club Kheybar Khorramabad in the Persian Gulf Pro League.

Grand Ayatollah Sheikh Hossein Vahid Khorasani (; born Mohammad-Hossein Molla-Saleh (Persian: محمدحسین ملاصالح); 1 January 1921) is an Iranian writer and Shia marja'. He was born in Nishapur, Iran. He is the head of the Qom Seminary. Khorasani is said to be the most learned Shia religious figure. His lectures and quotes have been used against the thinking of the supreme leader of Iran.

Hostel: Part III is the third installment in the Hostel horror movie series, directed by Scott Spiegel and released in 2011. Unlike the first two movies Hostel (2005) and Hostel: Part II (2007), which were set in Europe, this installment takes place in Las Vegas. The plot revolves around a group of friends who are in Las Vegas for a bachelor party. They encounter a mysterious and sinister organization that caters to wealthy clients looking to indulge in extreme and sadistic experiences. As the night unfolds, the friends find themselves trapped in a nightmare where their lives are at stake. The movie continues the franchise’s themes of torture and survival, showcasing graphic violence and psychological horror. It also explores the darker side of human nature and the consequences of unchecked desires.

Hot Mainstream Rock Tracks (originally called Mainstream Rock Tracks) is a ranking in Billboard of the most-played songs on mainstream rock radio stations, a category that includes stations that play primarily rock music but are not modern rock (that is, "alternative") stations, which are counted in the Hot Modern Rock Tracks chart.

Hotel for Dogs (1971) is a children's novel by Lois Duncan. It was made into a movie of the same name by DreamWorks Pictures. When the book was originally released in 1971, Andi's name was Liz, and Friday's name was Sadie. The book was re-released December 1, 2008, to promote the movie with the names changed. Two sequels were released: News for Dogs in 2009 and Movie for Dogs in 2010.

Hou Bo (; 17 September 1924 – 26 November 2017) was a Chinese photographer. With her husband Xu Xiaobing, they were among the best known photographers of Mao Zedong. She joined the Communist Party at the age of fourteen and learned photography during the Second Sino-Japanese War. After 1949, she and Xu Xiaobing lived in the same compound as Mao and took both official photos, some used for posters and publicity, which became the most widely circulated photos of Mao, and some family photos, taken informally behind the scenes. Among her best known photographs are "The Founding of the PRC" (1949), "Mao Zedong Swimming Across the Yangzi" (1955), "Chairman Mao at Work in an Airplane" (1959), and "Mao Zedong with Students from Latin America" (1959), which won First Prize in the National Photography Exhibition of 1959. Hou died on 26 November 2017 in Beijing at the age of 93.
House of Commons is the name of the lower house in several commonwealth parliaments The House of Commons of Southern Ireland (1921-1922) The House of Commons of Northern Ireland (1921-1971)
